$comment: Threads plan Part B: connections inside the Old Testament, one book per PR, each draft until the owner approves it. Every connection states its order (older end, use, basis).

connections.label: The Sabbath rests on the seventh day of creation
connections.explanation: Exodus 20:8–11 recalls Genesis 2:1–3: the Sabbath commandment gives as its reason the six days of making and God's rest on the seventh. Genesis says God finished his work, rested on the seventh day, blessed it and made it holy. The commandment says the LORD made heaven and earth in six days and rested, and therefore blessed the Sabbath and made it holy, with the same Hebrew word for the seventh day (below).

connections.label: The kings of Edom, listed twice
connections.explanation: 1 Chronicles 1:43–54 retells Genesis 36:31–43: the kings who reigned in Edom before Israel had a king, and the chiefs of Esau, name by name. The list opens with the same words in both books and runs through the same kings and cities, beginning with Bela son of Beor at Dinhabah, almost line for line. Rare names such as Dinhabah and Masrekah occur only in these two passages (below).

sources.author: Sara Japhet
sources.title: I & II Chronicles: A Commentary (Old Testament Library)

connections.label: Two blessings on Joseph
connections.explanation: Genesis 49:22–26 and Deuteronomy 33:13–17 both tell of a dying leader's blessing on Joseph, Jacob's and then Moses', in shared words. Both call down blessings of the heavens and of the deep that lies beneath, and both end on the same line: on the head of Joseph, on the crown of the one set apart from his brothers. The Hebrew words for the crown of the head and for the one set apart are shared (below); which blessing was written first is not stated.

connections.label: Is anything too hard for the LORD?
connections.explanation: Genesis 18:14 and Jeremiah 32:17–27 both tell that nothing is too hard for the LORD, once as his question to Abraham and once in Jeremiah's prayer and God's reply. In Genesis the LORD asks it when Sarah laughs at the promise of a son in her old age. In Jeremiah the prophet confesses it after buying a field, and the LORD answers with the same question; the Hebrew verb for being too hard is the same (below).

connections.label: Joseph's story sung
connections.explanation: Psalms 105:16–22 retells Genesis 37:2–41:57: Joseph sold as a slave, his feet in shackles, freed by the king and made ruler of his house. The psalm names Joseph and follows the story step by step: a famine, a man sent ahead, the word that proved him true, the king who set him free and put him over all his possessions. It tells each step as the LORD's own act: he called the famine and he sent the man.

connections.label: Blessed who blesses, cursed who curses
connections.explanation: Genesis 12:3 and Numbers 24:9 both tell that whoever blesses is blessed and whoever curses is cursed, first in God's promise to Abram and then in Balaam's oracle over Israel. Balaam, brought to curse Israel, ends his third oracle on the same pairing of blessing and curse. The Hebrew verb for cursing is the same in both (below).

connections.label: Abram called out of Ur
connections.explanation: Nehemiah 9:7–8 recalls Genesis 11:31–12:3: the great prayer of Nehemiah 9 confesses the LORD who chose Abram and brought him out of Ur of the Chaldees. Genesis tells of Terah leaving Ur with Abram and of the LORD's call to leave country and kindred for the land he would show. The prayer gathers this, the new name Abraham and the covenant to give the land into one confession; Ur of the Chaldees is named in both (below).

connections.label: Moriah
connections.explanation: 2 Chronicles 3:1 names the place of Genesis 22:2: Solomon builds the LORD's house on Mount Moriah. Genesis sends Abraham to the land of Moriah to offer Isaac on one of its mountains; Chronicles places the temple on Mount Moriah, at the threshing floor where the LORD appeared to David. Moriah is named in these two verses alone (below), and Chronicles does not mention Abraham, so the link is the place itself.

connections.label: A priest in the order of Melchizedek
connections.explanation: Psalms 110:4 names Melchizedek of Genesis 14:18–20: the LORD swears that the psalm's king is a priest forever in the order of Melchizedek. Genesis gives Melchizedek three verses, as king of Salem and priest of God Most High, who brings bread and wine and blesses Abram. Outside Genesis, the Old Testament names him only in this psalm (below).

connections.label: As when God overthrew Sodom and Gomorrah
connections.explanation: Amos 4:11 names the overthrow of Genesis 19:24–25: some of Israel were overthrown as when God overthrew Sodom and Gomorrah. Genesis tells how the LORD rained sulfur and fire on the two cities and overthrew them and all the plain. Amos uses the same verb for overthrowing (below), in a list of judgements after each of which Israel still did not return.

connections.label: Rulers of Sodom, people of Gomorrah
connections.explanation: Isaiah 1:9–10 names the cities of Genesis 19:24–25: only a small remnant kept Judah from becoming like Sodom and Gomorrah, and its rulers are then addressed as rulers of Sodom. Genesis tells of the two cities overthrown by fire. Isaiah turns their names first into a measure of near destruction and then into a charge against Jerusalem's leaders and people (the names below).

connections.label: Jacob took his brother by the heel
connections.explanation: Hosea 12:3 recalls Genesis 25:26: in the womb Jacob took his brother by the heel. Genesis tells it at the twins' birth, the second child coming out with his hand on Esau's heel and being named Jacob. Hosea recalls it in a charge against Jacob's descendants, setting their ancestor's grasping at birth beside his struggle with God.

connections.label: Jacob struggled with God and prevailed
connections.explanation: Hosea 12:3–4 recalls Genesis 32:24–30: in his manhood Jacob contended with God; he struggled with the angel and prevailed. Genesis tells of the night Jacob wrestled a man until daybreak, would not let him go without a blessing and was given the name Israel. Hosea adds that he wept and pleaded, and the verb for his struggling (below) occurs only in these two passages.

connections.label: The waters of Noah
connections.explanation: Isaiah 54:9 recalls Genesis 9:11–15: as God swore that the waters of Noah would never again cover the earth, so he swears not to be angry with Zion. Genesis tells of the covenant after the flood, sealed with the rainbow in the cloud. Isaiah takes that oath as the pattern for God's own oath to his people.

connections.label: Look to Abraham
connections.explanation: Isaiah 51:2 recalls Genesis 12:1–3: Zion is told to look to Abraham and Sarah, for God called Abraham when he was one man, blessed him and made him many. Genesis tells of the call to leave country and kindred and the promise of a great nation and a blessing. Isaiah offers that beginning as a reason to trust that God can do the same again.

connections.label: Jacob loved, Esau hated
connections.explanation: Malachi 1:2–3 recalls Genesis 25:23–34: Esau was Jacob's brother, yet the LORD loved Jacob and hated Esau. Genesis tells of the word to Rebekah that two nations were in her womb and the elder would serve the younger, and of Esau selling his birthright. Malachi answers Israel's question of how God has loved them by pointing to that choice and to the desolation of Esau's mountains.

connections.label: Rachel's tomb
connections.explanation: 1 Samuel 10:2 names the grave of Genesis 35:19–20: Samuel tells Saul he will meet two men by Rachel's tomb, on the border of Benjamin. Genesis tells of Rachel dying on the way to Ephrath and of Jacob setting up a pillar on her grave that stood to the writer's day. Samuel uses the tomb as a landmark on Saul's road home, with the same Hebrew word for the grave (below).

connections.label: The house of Perez
connections.explanation: Ruth 4:12 names the birth of Genesis 38:27–30: the elders bless Boaz's house to be like the house of Perez, whom Tamar bore to Judah. Genesis tells of the twins born to Tamar, the second breaking out first and named Perez. The book of Ruth ends with the line from Perez to David, so the blessing points to the family Ruth is joining (the name below).

connections.label: Joshua tells the story from Terah
connections.explanation: Joshua 24:2–4 retells Genesis 11:26–12:5: Terah beyond the River, Abraham taken from there and led through Canaan, then Isaac, Jacob and Esau. At Shechem Joshua opens the covenant by telling the story of Genesis in the LORD's own voice, down to Jacob's family going down into Egypt. Genesis does not say that Terah served other gods; Joshua's retelling adds it.

connections.label: Joseph's bones carried up
connections.explanation: Exodus 13:19 quotes Genesis 50:24–25: Moses takes Joseph's bones, because Joseph had made Israel swear that when God visited them they would carry his bones up. Exodus repeats Joseph's words almost exactly, so the oath sworn at his death is kept as Israel leaves Egypt. The Hebrew words for the visiting and for the bones are the same (below).

connections.label: The field at Shechem
connections.explanation: Joshua 24:32 recalls Genesis 33:19: Joseph's bones are buried at Shechem in the plot Jacob bought from the sons of Hamor for a hundred pieces of money. Genesis tells of Jacob buying the ground where he had spread his tent; Joshua names the same field, the same sellers and the same price, and it becomes the inheritance of Joseph's children. The rare word for the pieces of money (below) occurs only three times in the Old Testament.

connections.label: Formless and empty
connections.explanation: Genesis 1:2 and Jeremiah 4:23 both tell of the earth formless and empty, once before the first day and once in the prophet's vision of a land undone. Jeremiah adds that the heavens had no light, as before light was made. The second of the two Hebrew words occurs only three times in the Old Testament, twice here (below); which passage is the older is not stated.

connections.label: In Eden, the garden of God
connections.explanation: Ezekiel 28:13 names the garden of Genesis 2:8–15: the king of Tyre was in Eden, the garden of God, adorned with precious stones. Genesis places the garden in Eden, watered by a river that runs toward a land of gold, bdellium and onyx. Ezekiel's lament gives Tyre's king that garden's splendour before his fall, and Eden and the onyx are named in both (below).

connections.label: A king's dream, and the God who explains it
connections.explanation: Genesis 41:1–40 and Daniel 2:1–49 both tell of a foreign king troubled by a dream, his magicians unable to explain it, and a Hebrew captive who credits God and is raised to high office. Pharaoh's spirit is troubled and so is Nebuchadnezzar's; Joseph says the answer belongs to God, and Daniel says there is a God in heaven who reveals secrets. The Hebrew words for the troubled spirit and for the magicians are shared (below).

connections.label: Rule over the works of God's hands
connections.explanation: Genesis 1:26–28 and Psalms 8:4–8 both tell of humankind given rule over the creatures: the flocks and herds, the animals of the field, the birds of the sky and the fish of the sea. Genesis gives that rule at creation, with the image of God. The psalm marvels that God should care for so small a creature and has put all things under his feet.

connections.label: Noah, Daniel and Job
connections.explanation: Ezekiel 14:14 names Noah of Genesis 6:9: even Noah, Daniel and Job, were they in a guilty land, would save only themselves by their righteousness. Genesis calls Noah righteous and blameless among the people of his time. Ezekiel sets him beside two other righteous men to say that a land will not be spared for the sake of a few (the name below).

connections.label: The first Passover in the land
connections.explanation: Joshua 5:10–11 names the feast of Exodus 12:6: in Gilgal Israel keeps the Passover on the fourteenth day of the month at evening, as the law set it. Exodus fixes the lamb for the fourteenth day, killed at evening; Joshua records the first Passover kept in the land, on that day and at that hour, on the plains of Jericho. On the next day they eat the produce of the land.

connections.label: Jericho heard of the Red Sea
connections.explanation: Joshua 2:10 recalls Exodus 14:21–22: Rahab tells the spies that Jericho has heard of the LORD drying up the Red Sea before Israel. Exodus tells of the east wind that drove the sea back all night and made it dry ground. In Jericho the story has travelled ahead of Israel and is told back to them by a Canaanite woman.

connections.label: The Jordan dried up as the Red Sea was
connections.explanation: Joshua 4:23 recalls Exodus 14:21–22: the LORD dried up the Jordan before Israel as he had dried up the Red Sea. Exodus tells of the sea driven back and Israel crossing on dry ground with the waters a wall on either side. Joshua makes the crossing of the Jordan its second telling, so that children who ask about the stones will hear of both.

connections.label: The LORD is my strength and song
connections.explanation: Exodus 15:2 and Psalms 118:14 both tell that the LORD is my strength and song and has become my salvation, once in the Song of the Sea and once in a psalm of thanksgiving. The line is the same in the Hebrew, including a rare word for song (below), and Isaiah 12:2 has it too. Which was sung first is not stated.

connections.label: The manna ceased
connections.explanation: Joshua 5:12 recalls Exodus 16:35: the manna ceased the day after Israel ate the produce of Canaan. Exodus says Israel ate manna for forty years, until they came to the borders of the land of Canaan. Joshua records the day it stopped, at Gilgal, and the word for the manna is the same (below).

connections.label: As at Meribah, as at Massah
connections.explanation: Psalms 95:8–9 names the places of Exodus 17:7: the psalm warns against a hardened heart like Israel's at Meribah and Massah. Exodus names the place Massah and Meribah because the people quarrelled and tested the LORD, asking whether he was among them or not. The psalm turns the two names back into what they mean, testing and quarrelling, as a warning to those who sing it (below).

connections.label: The Ten Commandments, given twice
connections.explanation: Deuteronomy 5:6–21 retells Exodus 20:1–17: Moses repeats the Ten Commandments to the people about to enter the land. The commandments run in the same order with nearly the same words, and the Hebrew shares rare words such as those for the image and for coveting (below). Two differences stand out: Deuteronomy grounds the Sabbath in Israel's slavery in Egypt, where Exodus grounds it in the six days of creation, and it names the neighbour's wife before his house.

connections.label: The golden calf, remembered
connections.explanation: Deuteronomy 9:8–21 retells Exodus 32:1–20: Moses reminds Israel of the calf they made at Horeb while he stayed forty days on the mountain. Both tell of the molten calf, the LORD's anger and his word to let him destroy them, the tablets broken, and the calf burnt and ground to dust; the Hebrew for the molten image and for the grinding is shared (below). Deuteronomy adds that Moses fasted forty days and nights and prayed for Aaron too.

connections.label: A calf in Horeb
connections.explanation: Psalms 106:19–20 recalls Exodus 32:4: they made a calf in Horeb and worshipped a molten image. Exodus tells how Aaron fashioned the molten calf and the people hailed it as the gods who brought them out of Egypt. The psalm says that so they exchanged their glory for the image of a bull that eats grass, with the same words for the calf and the molten image (below).

connections.label: Moses prays God's own words back
connections.explanation: Numbers 14:17–19 quotes Exodus 34:6–7: after the spies' report Moses prays back to God the words God proclaimed of himself, slow to anger and abundant in loving kindness. Moses introduces them as what the LORD has spoken, keeps the line about forgiving iniquity and visiting it to the third and fourth generation, and asks pardon by the greatness of that loving kindness. The Hebrew for slow to anger and for clearing the guilty is the same (below).

connections.label: Merciful and gracious, slow to anger
connections.explanation: Exodus 34:6 and Jonah 4:2 both tell of a God merciful and gracious, slow to anger and abundant in loving kindness, once proclaimed at Sinai and once thrown back at God by an angry prophet. Jonah says he fled to Tarshish because he knew God was like this and would relent of doing harm. The Hebrew words for merciful and gracious are the same (below); which passage is the older is not stated.

connections.label: The cloud fills the dwelling
connections.explanation: Exodus 40:34–35 and 1 Kings 8:10–11 both tell of the cloud filling God's dwelling once it is finished, so that no one can go in. At the tabernacle Moses cannot enter because the cloud rests on it and the LORD's glory fills it; at the temple the priests cannot stand to minister because of the cloud, for the LORD's glory fills the house. The Hebrew words for the cloud and the glory are the same (below).

connections.label: Him who lived in the bush
connections.explanation: Deuteronomy 33:16 names the bush of Exodus 3:2–4: Moses blesses Joseph with the good will of him who lived in the bush. Exodus tells of the bush that burned and was not consumed, from which God called Moses. In his last blessing Moses names the LORD by that meeting, and the Hebrew word for this bush occurs only in these two passages (below).

connections.label: May his face shine on us
connections.explanation: Numbers 6:24–26 and Psalms 67:1 both tell of a prayer that God will bless and make his face shine, in the priests' blessing and in a psalm's opening. The psalm turns the blessing into the people's own request and goes on to ask that God's way be known on earth. The Hebrew words for shining and for being gracious are the same (below).

connections.label: Caleb remembers Kadesh Barnea
connections.explanation: Joshua 14:6–12 recalls Numbers 13:30–14:24: Caleb reminds Joshua of what the LORD said at Kadesh Barnea when the spies came back. Numbers tells of the twelve sent out, the frightened report of the many, Caleb's word that they could take the land, and the LORD's promise that Caleb, who followed him fully, would enter it. Forty-five years later Caleb, still strong, asks for the hill country that promise gave him.

connections.label: The earth opened for Dathan and Abiram
connections.explanation: Psalms 106:16–18 recalls Numbers 16:31–33: the earth opened for Dathan and Abiram, who had envied Moses and Aaron. Numbers tells of the ground splitting under Korah's men and their households, who went down alive to Sheol. The psalm names Dathan and Abiram and the fire that burned the wicked, in its long confession of Israel's sins, with the same verb for swallowing (below).

connections.label: Moses at the waters of Meribah
connections.explanation: Psalms 106:32–33 recalls Numbers 20:10–13: at the waters of Meribah Moses was troubled for Israel's sake and spoke rashly. Numbers tells of Moses striking the rock twice and of the LORD's word that, because he did not believe or honour him, he would not lead the people into the land. The psalm lays the cause on the people's rebellion, which made Moses speak rashly with his lips (the place's name below).

connections.label: The bronze serpent broken
connections.explanation: 2 Kings 18:4 names the serpent of Numbers 21:8–9: Hezekiah broke in pieces the bronze serpent Moses had made, because Israel burned incense to it. Numbers tells how Moses set a bronze serpent on a pole so that whoever was bitten and looked at it lived. Kings records its end long after, when it had become an object of worship called Nehushtan, with the same words for serpent and bronze (below).

connections.label: Balaam sent for to curse
connections.explanation: Joshua 24:9–10 recalls Numbers 22:5–6: Balak king of Moab sent for Balaam son of Beor to curse Israel, but the LORD would not listen to Balaam. Numbers tells of the messengers sent to Pethor by the River and of Balak's plea for a curse on a people too mighty for him. In Joshua's covenant speech the LORD tells the outcome in a line, that Balaam blessed Israel instead (the names below).

connections.label: Remember what Balak devised
connections.explanation: Micah 6:5 recalls Numbers 22:5–6: Israel is told to remember what Balak devised and what Balaam son of Beor answered him. Numbers tells of the king of Moab sending for the seer to curse a people too mighty for him. Micah sets the story among the LORD's righteous acts, in his case against his own people (the names below).

connections.label: Phinehas stood up
connections.explanation: Psalms 106:28–31 recalls Numbers 25:7–13: when Israel joined Baal Peor and a plague broke out, Phinehas stood up and the plague was stopped. Numbers tells of Phinehas's spear and of the covenant of a lasting priesthood given him for his zeal. The psalm says the act was credited to him as righteousness for all generations, and names him with the same word for the plague (below).

connections.label: Birds for the craving
connections.explanation: Psalms 78:26–31 retells Numbers 11:31–34: God sent a wind that brought birds down around the camp, and while the food was still in their mouths his anger struck them. Numbers tells of the quail let fall around the camp and gathered for two days, and of the plague that named the place for the graves of those who craved. The psalm keeps the order and makes it a lesson about desire that was granted and then judged.

connections.label: Moses laid his hands on Joshua
connections.explanation: Deuteronomy 34:9 recalls Numbers 27:18–23: Joshua, on whom Moses had laid his hands, is filled with wisdom and Israel listens to him. Numbers tells of the LORD's command to take Joshua, a man in whom is the Spirit, lay a hand on him and commission him before Eleazar and the congregation so that Israel would obey him. At Moses' death Deuteronomy records that it was so, with the same verb for laying on hands (below).

connections.label: The cities of refuge
connections.explanation: Joshua 20:1–3 recalls Numbers 35:9–15: the LORD tells Joshua to assign the cities of refuge of which he spoke by Moses. Numbers sets out cities to which one who killed a person unintentionally could flee from the avenger until judged. Joshua repeats the law's terms, the unwitting killer and the avenger of blood, and then names the cities (the words below).

connections.label: The eastern tribes held to their word
connections.explanation: Joshua 1:12–15 recalls Numbers 32:20–22: Joshua reminds Reuben, Gad and half of Manasseh of the word Moses commanded them. In Numbers they ask to settle east of the Jordan, and Moses agrees on condition that their armed men cross over and fight until the land is subdued. Before the crossing Joshua holds them to it.

connections.label: With all his heart, soul and might
connections.explanation: 2 Kings 23:25 recalls Deuteronomy 6:4–5: Josiah turned to the LORD with all his heart, soul and might, according to all the law of Moses. Deuteronomy commands Israel to love the LORD with heart, soul and might; Kings gives Josiah the same three, and says no king before or after was like him. The full three-part phrase, ending with might, occurs nowhere else in the Old Testament.

connections.label: A king like all the nations
connections.explanation: Deuteronomy 17:14–15 and 1 Samuel 8:5 both tell of Israel asking for a king like all the nations around. Deuteronomy foresees the request and allows a king of the LORD's choosing, one of their own brothers. In Samuel the elders make the request, and the LORD tells Samuel that it is he they have rejected.

connections.label: Each shall die for his own sin
connections.explanation: 2 Kings 14:6 quotes Deuteronomy 24:16: Amaziah spared the children of his father's murderers, as written in the book of the law of Moses. Kings gives the law in full, that fathers shall not die for their children nor children for their fathers, but each for his own sin. It names the book of the law of Moses as its source (the word for sin below).

connections.label: No Ammonite or Moabite in the assembly
connections.explanation: Nehemiah 13:1–2 quotes Deuteronomy 23:3–5: the book of Moses, read to the people, says no Ammonite or Moabite may enter the assembly of God. Deuteronomy gives the reasons, that they did not meet Israel with bread and water and hired Balaam to curse them, and adds that God turned the curse into a blessing. Nehemiah repeats all three, with the same Hebrew words (below), and the people separate from those of foreign descent.

connections.label: The curse written in the law of Moses
connections.explanation: Daniel 9:11–13 names the curse of Deuteronomy 28:15–68: Daniel confesses that the curse and the oath written in the law of Moses have been poured out on Israel. Deuteronomy sets out the curses that will overtake Israel if it does not listen to the LORD's voice. Daniel's prayer confesses that this has happened, the great evil that came on Jerusalem coming as Moses wrote.

connections.label: Scatter and gather
connections.explanation: Nehemiah 1:8–9 quotes Deuteronomy 30:1–4: Nehemiah asks God to remember his word to Moses, to scatter Israel if they sinned and to gather them if they returned. Deuteronomy promises that if the scattered return to the LORD with all their heart he will gather them even from the farthest parts of heaven. Nehemiah prays it back in the words of the promise (below), ending at the place God chose for his name.

connections.label: Be strong and courageous
connections.explanation: Joshua 1:5–9 echoes Deuteronomy 31:6–8: the LORD tells Joshua what Moses had told him, to be strong and courageous, for God will not fail or forsake him. In Deuteronomy Moses charges Joshua before all Israel. In Joshua the LORD repeats the charge after Moses' death and adds that he will be with Joshua as he was with Moses, in the same Hebrew words (below).

connections.label: Admah and Zeboiim
connections.explanation: Deuteronomy 29:23 and Hosea 11:8 both tell of Admah and Zeboiim, cities overthrown with Sodom and Gomorrah. Deuteronomy holds up their overthrow as what a faithless land will become; Hosea has God ask how he can make Ephraim like them, and his compassion is stirred. The two names are rare (below); which passage is the older is not stated.

connections.label: The place he chooses for his name
connections.explanation: Deuteronomy 12:5 and 1 Kings 8:29 both tell of the place the LORD chooses for his name. Deuteronomy commands Israel to seek the place God will choose out of all their tribes to put his name there. At the temple's dedication Solomon prays toward the house of which God said that his name would be there.

connections.label: Jericho rebuilt at a cost
connections.explanation: 1 Kings 16:34 shows Joshua 6:26 fulfilled: Hiel of Bethel rebuilt Jericho at the cost of his firstborn and his youngest son, according to the LORD's word spoken by Joshua. Joshua laid a curse on whoever rebuilt the city, that he would lose his firstborn when he laid its foundation and his youngest son when he hung its gates. Kings records it in the same terms, naming the sons Abiram and Segub, with the same words for foundation and youngest (below).

connections.label: The valley of Achor, a door of hope
connections.explanation: Hosea 2:15 names the valley of Joshua 7:24–26: God will make the valley of Achor a door of hope. Joshua tells how Achan, who took the devoted things, was stoned in that valley, named for the trouble he brought on Israel. Hosea promises that the place of that trouble will become an entrance to hope, as in the day Israel came up out of Egypt (the name below).

connections.label: Achar, the troubler of Israel
connections.explanation: 1 Chronicles 2:7 names Achan of Joshua 7:1: in Judah's genealogy the son of Carmi is Achar, the troubler of Israel, who trespassed in the devoted thing. Joshua names him Achan son of Carmi, of the tribe of Judah, who took some of the devoted things. Chronicles spells his name to match the trouble he caused and keeps only that deed, with the same words for Carmi and the trespass (below).

connections.label: Sun and moon stood still
connections.explanation: Joshua 10:12–14 and Habakkuk 3:11 both tell of the sun and moon standing still in the sky at the LORD's battle. In Joshua it is the answer to Joshua's word at Gibeon, so that the day lasted until Israel had defeated its enemies. Habakkuk's prayer sees sun and moon halted at the light of God's arrows, with the same words for sun and moon (below).

connections.label: The oath to the Gibeonites
connections.explanation: 2 Samuel 21:1–2 recalls Joshua 9:15–20: a three-year famine comes because Saul put the Gibeonites to death, though Israel had sworn to them. Joshua tells how the princes of Israel, deceived, swore an oath to let the Gibeonites live and kept it once the truth came out. Samuel explains that the Gibeonites were not Israelites but a remnant of the Amorites, protected by that oath.

connections.label: Not one good word failed
connections.explanation: Joshua 21:43–45 and 1 Kings 8:56 both tell that not one of the LORD's good promises to Israel failed, once at the end of the conquest and once at the temple's dedication. Joshua says the LORD gave the land and rest all around, and every word came to pass. Solomon blesses the LORD for giving rest to his people, for not one word of his promise by Moses has failed, with the same verb for failing (below).

connections.label: The Jordan driven back
connections.explanation: Psalms 114:3–5 recalls Joshua 3:14–17: the sea saw and fled, the Jordan was driven back. Joshua tells of the waters of the Jordan standing up in a heap when the priests' feet touched them. The psalm sets the Jordan beside the sea of the exodus and asks them both what made them turn back.

connections.label: As at the rock of Oreb
connections.explanation: Isaiah 10:26 recalls Judges 7:19–25: the LORD will strike Assyria as in the slaughter of Midian at the rock of Oreb. Judges tells of Gideon's night attack with trumpets and torches, the rout of Midian and the death of its prince Oreb at the rock that bears his name. Isaiah makes it a pattern for God's judgement on Assyria, beside the rod lifted over the sea (the names below).

connections.label: Like Oreb and Zeeb
connections.explanation: Psalms 83:9–11 recalls Judges 7:19–25: the psalm asks God to make Israel's enemies like Oreb and Zeeb, princes of Midian. Judges tells of Midian's defeat and of the princes Oreb and Zeeb killed at the rock and the winepress named for them. The psalm prays for the same end to a new alliance gathered against Israel (the names below).

connections.label: As to Sisera and Jabin
connections.explanation: Psalms 83:9–10 recalls Judges 4:15–21: do to them as to Sisera and Jabin at the river Kishon. Judges tells how the LORD threw Sisera's chariots into confusion before Barak and how Sisera, fleeing on foot, died in Jael's tent. The psalm sets that victory beside Gideon's over Midian (the names below).

connections.label: The cycle of the judges, confessed
connections.explanation: Nehemiah 9:26–28 retells Judges 2:11–19: Israel rebelled, God gave them into their enemies' hands, they cried out and he sent saviours, and again they did evil. Judges sets out the cycle at the start of the book, from serving the Baals to the judges raised up and the people turning back once each judge died. The prayer of Nehemiah 9 tells the same cycle in the same order as part of its confession, with the same word for their distress (below).

connections.label: Fables of trees and thistles
connections.explanation: Judges 9:8–15 and 2 Kings 14:9 both tell of a fable in which plants speak, told to put an overreaching ruler in his place. Jotham tells of the trees seeking a king and the bramble that accepts; Jehoash king of Israel answers Amaziah's challenge with a thistle in Lebanon that asks a cedar for his daughter. They are the two plant fables of the historical books, with the cedars of Lebanon in both (below).

connections.label: As in the days of Gibeah
connections.explanation: Hosea 9:9 recalls Judges 19:22–30: Israel has corrupted itself as in the days of Gibeah. Judges tells of the crime at Gibeah, the abuse and death of the Levite's concubine, which the Israelites said had no equal since the exodus. Hosea makes the days of Gibeah the measure of Israel's corruption in his own time.

connections.label: No razor on his head
connections.explanation: Judges 13:5 and 1 Samuel 1:11 both tell of a child given to God from birth, on whose head no razor shall come. The angel tells Samson's mother that her son will be a Nazirite from the womb; Hannah vows that if the LORD gives her a son, he will be the LORD's all his days, with the same promise about the razor. The word for the razor occurs only three times in the Old Testament (below).

connections.label: From Perez to David
connections.explanation: Ruth 4:18–22 and 1 Chronicles 2:4–15 both tell of the line from Perez to David: Hezron, Ram, Amminadab, Nahshon, Salmon, Boaz, Obed and Jesse. Ruth closes with these ten generations as the book's last word; Chronicles sets them inside the larger family of Judah. The names match generation by generation (below); which list is the older is not stated.

connections.label: Like Rachel and Leah
connections.explanation: Ruth 4:11 names the mothers of Genesis 29:31–30:24: the elders bless Ruth to be like Rachel and Leah, who both built the house of Israel. Genesis tells of the sons born to Leah and Rachel and their maids, the rivalry between the sisters, and the LORD who opened their wombs. Ruth's blessing joins the two rivals as the builders of one house (the names below).

connections.label: The sandal at the gate
connections.explanation: Deuteronomy 25:7–10 and Ruth 4:7–8 both tell of a sandal taken off to settle a kinsman's duty before the elders at the town gate. Deuteronomy sets the shame of the sandal on a brother who refuses to raise up a name for his dead brother. In Ruth the nearer kinsman gives up his right to redeem by drawing off his own sandal, a custom of former times, with the same word for sandal (below).

connections.label: He raises the poor from the dust
connections.explanation: 1 Samuel 2:1–10 and Psalms 113:7–9 both tell of the LORD who lifts the poor from the dust and the needy from the ash heap to sit with princes. Hannah sings it when Samuel is born, after years of barrenness; the psalm adds that God gives the barren woman a home as a joyful mother of children. The word for the ash heap occurs only three times in the Old Testament, twice here (below).

connections.label: Not sacrifice
connections.explanation: 1 Samuel 15:22 and Hosea 6:6 both tell that God wants more than sacrifice: obedience in Samuel's rebuke of Saul, mercy and the knowledge of God in Hosea. Samuel asks whether the LORD delights in burnt offerings as much as in obeying his voice. Hosea has God say he desires mercy rather than sacrifice and the knowledge of himself more than burnt offerings, with the same two words (below).

connections.label: Taken from the sheepfolds
connections.explanation: Psalms 78:70–72 recalls 1 Samuel 16:11–13: God chose David his servant and took him from the sheepfolds to shepherd his people. Samuel tells how the youngest son, out keeping the sheep, was sent for and anointed. The psalm ends its long history at that point, with the shepherd boy made Israel's shepherd.

connections.label: Saul's death on Gilboa, told twice
connections.explanation: 1 Chronicles 10:1–14 retells 1 Samuel 31:1–13: the Philistines defeat Israel on Mount Gilboa, Saul's sons fall, and Saul dies by his own sword. Chronicles follows Samuel almost word for word, down to the men of Jabesh who recover the bodies, with the same names and places (below). It then adds its own judgement: Saul died for his unfaithfulness and for consulting a medium instead of the LORD.

sources.author: Sara Japhet
sources.title: I & II Chronicles: A Commentary (Old Testament Library)

connections.label: Go to Shiloh and see
connections.explanation: Jeremiah 7:12–14 recalls 1 Samuel 4:10–11: go to Shiloh, where God first set his name, and see what he did to it. Samuel tells of the battle in which the ark was taken and Eli's sons were killed. Jeremiah, standing in the temple, warns that this house can go the way of Shiloh.

connections.label: The glory given into captivity
connections.explanation: Psalms 78:60–64 retells 1 Samuel 4:10–22: God abandoned the tent of Shiloh and gave his strength into captivity, his glory into the enemy's hand. Samuel tells of the ark taken, Eli's sons killed and the child named for the glory departed from Israel. The psalm tells it as God's judgement, priests falling by the sword and widows unable to weep (the place below).

connections.label: Nathan's promise, told twice
connections.explanation: 1 Chronicles 17:11–14 retells 2 Samuel 7:12–16: Nathan's word to David that God will raise up his offspring, establish his throne forever and be a father to him. Chronicles follows Samuel closely but leaves out the warning that the son will be punished with the rod of men if he does wrong. It also speaks of God's own house and kingdom where Samuel speaks of David's.

sources.author: Sara Japhet
sources.title: I & II Chronicles: A Commentary (Old Testament Library)

connections.label: Sworn to David
connections.explanation: Psalms 89:3–4 recalls 2 Samuel 7:12–16: God has sworn to David his servant to establish his offspring forever and build up his throne. Samuel tells of Nathan's promise of a house, a kingdom and a throne forever. The psalm calls it a covenant sworn to David and later holds God to it when the king is defeated.

connections.label: David's song, twice
connections.explanation: 2 Samuel 22:1–51 and Psalms 18:1–50 both tell David's song of deliverance from his enemies and from Saul: the same song twice. Line by line they are almost the same, from the LORD as rock, fortress and deliverer to the cords of death and God riding on a cherub, and they share even rare words (below). They differ in small wordings, and the psalm opens with a line of love for the LORD.

connections.label: Except in the matter of Uriah
connections.explanation: 1 Kings 15:5 recalls 2 Samuel 11:2–27: David did right in the LORD's eyes all his days, except in the matter of Uriah the Hittite. Samuel tells of David taking Bathsheba, Uriah's wife, and sending Uriah to die in battle. Kings, measuring David's heirs against him, names that one exception (below).

connections.label: The stronghold of Zion taken
connections.explanation: 1 Chronicles 11:4–9 retells 2 Samuel 5:6–10: David takes the stronghold of Zion from the Jebusites, and it becomes the city of David. Chronicles follows Samuel closely, with the same rare words for the stronghold and the Millo (below). It adds that Joab went up first and became chief, and leaves out the saying about the blind and the lame.

sources.author: Sara Japhet
sources.title: I & II Chronicles: A Commentary (Old Testament Library)

connections.label: David's census, told twice
connections.explanation: 1 Chronicles 21:1–30 retells 2 Samuel 24:1–25: David's census, the plague and the threshing floor bought for an altar. The two accounts differ at the start: in Samuel the LORD's anger moves David to count Israel, and in Chronicles Satan moves him. Chronicles names the owner of the threshing floor Ornan and gives a higher price, and the seer Gad is named in both (below).

sources.author: Sara Japhet
sources.title: I & II Chronicles: A Commentary (Old Testament Library)

connections.label: The ark brought up with joy
connections.explanation: 1 Chronicles 15:25–16:3 retells 2 Samuel 6:12–19: David brings the ark up from the house of Obed-Edom with joy and dancing, while Michal looks down from a window. Chronicles follows Samuel's account, down to a rare word for the portion each person received (below). It adds the Levites who carried the ark and the singers, in keeping with its interest in the temple's service.

sources.author: Sara Japhet
sources.title: I & II Chronicles: A Commentary (Old Testament Library)

connections.label: The temple dedicated, told twice
connections.explanation: 2 Chronicles 5:2–6:11 retells 1 Kings 8:1–21: the ark brought into the temple, the cloud that filled the house, and Solomon's words at its dedication. Chronicles follows Kings closely, keeping its rare words for the inner sanctuary and for the thick darkness where the LORD dwells (below). It adds the Levite singers, whose praise comes just before the cloud fills the house.

sources.author: Sara Japhet
sources.title: I & II Chronicles: A Commentary (Old Testament Library)

connections.label: Solomon asks for wisdom
connections.explanation: 2 Chronicles 1:3–13 retells 1 Kings 3:4–15: at Gibeon God tells Solomon to ask for what he wants, and Solomon asks for wisdom to govern. Both give God's answer that since he did not ask for riches, honour or a long life, he will have wisdom and the rest besides, with the same Hebrew for Gibeon and the riches (below). Chronicles explains why Gibeon, where the tent of meeting stood, and does not call the meeting a dream.

sources.author: Sara Japhet
sources.title: I & II Chronicles: A Commentary (Old Testament Library)

connections.label: The queen of Sheba, told twice
connections.explanation: 2 Chronicles 9:1–12 retells 1 Kings 10:1–13: the queen of Sheba tests Solomon with hard questions, sees his wisdom and his house, and blesses his God. Chronicles keeps the account almost word for word, down to rare words for the attendants' standing and their clothing (below).

sources.author: Sara Japhet
sources.title: I & II Chronicles: A Commentary (Old Testament Library)

connections.label: The kingdom divided, told twice
connections.explanation: 2 Chronicles 10:1–19 retells 1 Kings 12:1–20: Rehoboam refuses to lighten the yoke Solomon laid on Israel, and the northern tribes break away. Both keep the young men's advice, scorpions in place of whips, and both say the turn came from God to fulfil Ahijah's word to Jeroboam (the rare words below).

sources.author: Sara Japhet
sources.title: I & II Chronicles: A Commentary (Old Testament Library)

connections.label: Josiah, named before his birth
connections.explanation: 2 Kings 23:15–18 shows 1 Kings 13:1–2 fulfilled: Josiah burns bones on the altar at Bethel, as the man of God from Judah had cried out against it. Kings tells of a man of God who, in Jeroboam's day, named a future king of David's house, Josiah, who would burn human bones on that altar. About three centuries later Josiah does it and spares only the tomb of the man of God who foretold it (the names below).

connections.label: In the rock, as the LORD passes by
connections.explanation: Exodus 33:21–23 and 1 Kings 19:9–13 both tell of the LORD passing by a prophet sheltered in the rock at God's mountain. Moses is set in a cleft of the rock and covered by God's hand while his glory passes. Elijah, in a cave at Horeb, hears the LORD pass by not in the wind, the earthquake or the fire but in a still small voice, and covers his face with his mantle.

connections.label: The blood of Naboth repaid
connections.explanation: 2 Kings 9:25–26 shows 1 Kings 21:17–24 fulfilled: Jehu has Joram's body thrown into Naboth's field, to repay the blood of Naboth as the LORD had said. Kings tells how Elijah, after Naboth was killed for his vineyard, met Ahab there and declared the LORD's sentence on his house. Jehu recalls hearing that word himself, riding behind Ahab, and carries it out on Ahab's son (the name below).

connections.label: The dogs at Jezreel
connections.explanation: 2 Kings 9:36–37 shows 1 Kings 21:23 fulfilled: the dogs eat Jezebel's flesh at Jezreel, as the LORD spoke by Elijah. Elijah's sentence on Ahab's house includes the queen who arranged Naboth's death. After Jehu has her thrown from a window, he recalls the word and says it has come to pass (the names below).

connections.label: Micaiah against the four hundred
connections.explanation: 2 Chronicles 18:1–34 retells 1 Kings 22:1–40: Micaiah, alone against four hundred prophets, foretells Ahab's death at Ramoth Gilead, and Ahab dies in disguise. Chronicles copies Kings closely, the vision of the LORD's host and the lying spirit included, with rare words found only in these chapters (below). It tells the story within Jehoshaphat's reign and adds that God helped Jehoshaphat when he cried out.

sources.author: Sara Japhet
sources.title: I & II Chronicles: A Commentary (Old Testament Library)

connections.label: Even Solomon
connections.explanation: Nehemiah 13:26 recalls 1 Kings 11:1–8: Solomon, loved by his God, was led into sin by foreign women. Kings tells of Solomon's many foreign wives, from nations the LORD had forbidden, who turned his heart to other gods in his old age. Nehemiah uses the warning against men of his own day who had married women of Ashdod, Ammon and Moab (the word for foreign below).

connections.label: Sennacherib at the gates, told twice
connections.explanation: 2 Kings 18:13–19:37 and Isaiah 36:1–37:38 both tell of Sennacherib's siege, the Rabshakeh's speech at the wall, Hezekiah's prayer and Isaiah's answer, and the Assyrian army struck in the night. The two accounts are almost word for word the same and share names found only here (below). Kings also records that Hezekiah first paid tribute, which Isaiah's account leaves out; which account is the older is not stated.

connections.label: Hezekiah's illness, told twice
connections.explanation: 2 Kings 20:1–11 and Isaiah 38:1–8 both tell of Hezekiah's illness, his prayer with tears, fifteen more years, and the shadow turned back on the steps. Kings has Isaiah order a cake of figs and Hezekiah ask for the sign; Isaiah's book places those details at the end and adds the psalm Hezekiah wrote when he recovered. The words for the tears and for the shadow going backward are the same (below).

connections.label: Josiah's reform, told twice
connections.explanation: 2 Chronicles 34:1–35:27 retells 2 Kings 22:1–23:30: Josiah's reform, the book of the law found in the temple, Huldah's word, the covenant, the Passover and his death at Megiddo. Chronicles follows Kings, with names found only in these chapters (below), but puts Josiah's purge of idols before the finding of the book. It gives his Passover at great length and says he died for not listening to God's word through Pharaoh Neco.

sources.author: Sara Japhet
sources.title: I & II Chronicles: A Commentary (Old Testament Library)

connections.label: Jerusalem's fall, told twice
connections.explanation: 2 Kings 25:1–21 and Jeremiah 52:4–27 both tell of Jerusalem's fall: the siege and famine, Zedekiah blinded at Riblah, the temple burnt and its bronze carried to Babylon. The two accounts match almost word for word and share rare words found only in these chapters (below). Jeremiah's chapter goes on to count those taken into exile; which account is the older is not stated.

connections.label: Jehoiachin released
connections.explanation: 2 Kings 25:27–30 and Jeremiah 52:31–34 both tell, at the end of their books, of Jehoiachin released from prison in Babylon in the thirty-seventh year of his exile and seated at the king's table. The two accounts differ only in the day of the month: the twenty-seventh in Kings, the twenty-fifth in Jeremiah. The name of the king who freed him occurs only in these passages (below).

connections.label: The temple vessels returned
connections.explanation: Ezra 1:7–11 recalls 2 Kings 24:13: Cyrus brings out the vessels of the LORD's house that Nebuchadnezzar had carried away. Kings tells how Nebuchadnezzar carried off the treasures of the temple and cut up the gold vessels Solomon had made. Ezra lists the vessels Cyrus returned, counted out to Sheshbazzar for the journey home.

connections.label: Taken up in a storm of fire
connections.explanation: Sirach 48:9–12 recalls 2 Kings 2:1–12: Elijah was taken up in a storm of fire by a chariot with horses of fire. Kings tells of Elijah's last walk with Elisha from Gilgal to the Jordan and of the chariot and whirlwind that took him. Sirach's praise of the ancestors recalls it and joins it to the hope that Elijah will come to turn the hearts of fathers to their sons.

connections.label: Jonah son of Amittai
connections.explanation: Jonah 1:1 names the prophet of 2 Kings 14:25: the LORD's word comes to Jonah son of Amittai. Kings mentions Jonah son of Amittai, the prophet from Gath Hepher, whose word was fulfilled when Jeroboam the second restored Israel's border. The book of Jonah opens with the same name and father, and Amittai is named only in these two verses (below).

connections.label: Mordecai among the exiles
connections.explanation: Esther 2:5–6 recalls 2 Kings 24:14–15: Mordecai, a Benjamite in Susa, had been carried away from Jerusalem by Nebuchadnezzar. Kings tells of Nebuchadnezzar deporting Jehoiachin, the princes and the craftsmen to Babylon. Esther places Mordecai's family among those exiles.

connections.label: The word by Jeremiah's mouth
connections.explanation: Ezra 1:1 shows Jeremiah 29:10 fulfilled: Cyrus's decree comes so that the LORD's word by Jeremiah's mouth might be accomplished. Jeremiah's letter to the exiles promises that after seventy years for Babylon God will visit them and bring them back to this place. Ezra opens the return by naming Jeremiah as the word now coming true.

connections.label: Daniel reads Jeremiah's seventy years
connections.explanation: Daniel 9:2 names the prophecy of Jeremiah 25:11–12: Daniel understands from the books the seventy years of Jerusalem's desolations, as the LORD's word came to Jeremiah. Jeremiah foretells that the land will be a desolation and the nations will serve Babylon seventy years. Daniel, reading it in the first year of Darius, turns to prayer, and the angel answers with seventy weeks of years (the shared words below).

connections.label: Seventy years of Sabbath
connections.explanation: 2 Chronicles 36:21 names the prophecy of Jeremiah 25:11–12: the land lay desolate and kept its Sabbaths to fulfil seventy years, by the word of the LORD through Jeremiah. Jeremiah foretells seventy years of desolation and of service to Babylon. Chronicles reads them as the Sabbaths the land had not been given, the rest the law had warned the land would take while Israel was in exile.

connections.label: Cyrus's decree, twice
connections.explanation: Ezra 1:1–3 and 2 Chronicles 36:22–23 both tell of Cyrus's decree in the first year of his reign: the LORD stirred his spirit to build him a house in Jerusalem, and his people may go up. Chronicles ends with the decree, breaking off in mid-sentence at let him go up, and Ezra begins with it in full, word for word (below). Which book took it from the other is not stated.

connections.label: Cyrus, who will say of Jerusalem: let it be built
connections.explanation: Isaiah 44:28 and Ezra 1:1–2 both tell of Cyrus as the one through whom Jerusalem and its temple will be built. Isaiah has the LORD call Cyrus his shepherd, who will say of Jerusalem that it shall be built and of the temple that its foundation shall be laid. Ezra records Cyrus's decree that the LORD has charged him to build him a house in Jerusalem.

connections.label: The peoples of the lands
connections.explanation: Ezra 9:1–2 recalls Deuteronomy 7:1–3: the leaders report that Israel has not kept itself apart from the peoples of the lands, the Canaanites, Hittites, Perizzites, Jebusites and others. Deuteronomy lists the nations of the land and forbids marrying with them. Ezra's report names the same peoples (below) and says the holy offspring have mixed with them.

connections.label: The register of the returned, twice
connections.explanation: Ezra 2:1–70 and Nehemiah 7:6–73 both tell the list of those who returned from exile with Zerubbabel, family by family and town by town. Nehemiah says he found the register of those who came up first and sets it out; the two lists match name for name, with small differences in some of the numbers (rare names below). Which book holds the earlier copy is not stated.

connections.label: Booths, found written in the law
connections.explanation: Nehemiah 8:14–17 quotes Leviticus 23:39–43: the people find written in the law that Israel should live in booths during the feast of the seventh month. Leviticus commands the feast with branches of trees, as a memorial that Israel lived in booths after the exodus. Nehemiah tells how the people gathered branches, built booths on roofs and in courtyards, and kept the feast as they had not since Joshua's day (the shared words below).

connections.label: The sea divided, confessed
connections.explanation: Nehemiah 9:9–11 recalls Exodus 14:21–28: God divided the sea before Israel so that they passed through on dry ground, and threw their pursuers into the depths. Exodus tells of the east wind, the dry ground and the waters returning on Pharaoh's army. The prayer of Nehemiah 9 tells it with the same words for the dry ground and the dividing (below), the pursuers thrown like a stone into mighty waters.

connections.label: Sihon and Og
connections.explanation: Nehemiah 9:22 recalls Numbers 21:21–35: Israel took the land of Sihon king of Heshbon and the land of Og king of Bashan. Numbers tells of the two kings who would not let Israel pass and were defeated east of the Jordan. The prayer of Nehemiah 9 counts their lands among the kingdoms God gave (the names below).

connections.label: Bread from heaven, confessed
connections.explanation: Nehemiah 9:15 recalls Exodus 16:4–15: God gave Israel bread from heaven for their hunger. Exodus tells of the LORD raining bread from heaven, the manna the people did not recognise. The prayer of Nehemiah 9 joins it to the water brought out of the rock and the command to go in and possess the land.

connections.label: For he is good
connections.explanation: Psalms 136:1 and Ezra 3:10–11 both tell the same refrain of thanks: the LORD is good, and his loving kindness endures forever. Psalm 136 repeats the second half after every line of Israel's story. At the founding of the second temple the priests and Levites sing it to one another, the people shout, and some who had seen the first house weep.
